# Human naive B cells recognize pre-pandemic influenza virus hemagglutinins

**Authors:** Jared Feldman; Ana Sofia Ferreira Ramos; Mya Vu; Daniel P. Maurer; Victoria C. Rosado; Daniel Lingwood; Goran Bajic; Aaron G. Schmidt

**Affiliations:** 1Ragon Institute of Mass General, MIT, and Harvard, Cambridge, MA, 02139, USA | 2Department of Microbiology, Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, New York, NY 10029 | 3Department of Microbiology, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA 02115, USA

## Abstract

Understanding the naïve B cell repertoire and its specificity for potential zoonotic threats, such as the highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) H5Nx viruses may allow prediction of infection- or vaccine-specific responses. However, this naïve repertoire and the possibility to respond to emerging, pre-pandemic viruses is largely undetermined. Here, we profiled naive B cell reactivity against a prototypical HPAI H5 hemagglutinin (HA), the major target of antibody responses. We find that the frequency of H5-specific human naive B cells targeting the HA “head” domain was increased relative to cross-reactive B cells to a circulating seasonal H1N1 strain. We classified the isolated monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) by the HA epitopes engaged and found selected mAbs neutralized H5N1 at germline. We determined a cryo-EM structure of one mAb in complex with H5 HA to define its epitope. Our study defines the naive human B cell repertoire recognizing a potentially zoonotic HPAI.

## Abstract

Naive antibodies targeting the influenza hemagglutinin from potentially pandemic H5Nx viruses can be isolated from individuals.

## INTRODUCTION

The seasonal antigenic drift and the pandemic antigenic shift of the major influenza virus surface glycoproteins, hemagglutinin (HA) and neuraminidase (NA), present a moving target for long-lasting antibody-mediated immunity and pose a constant public health threat. Evolutionary pressure exerted by host humoral responses causes viral immune evasion through mutations that arise principally around the periphery of the HA receptor binding site (1, 2) but can also occur outside this region; annual updates to seasonal vaccines to match the circulating strains are thus required. Seasonal vaccines can elicit or boost strain-specific antibody responses to currently circulating viruses, including H1, H3, and B influenzas (3). However, these seasonal vaccines do not afford protection against viruses with pandemic potential, such as H5Nx and H7Nx subtypes, to which the human population is largely naive (4). Highly pathogenetic avian influenza (HPAI) H5Nx strains circulate widely in wild avian populations, cause frequent domestic poultry outbreaks, and can infect humans upon acquisition of mutations that favor the binding to human sialic acid receptors (5). While no cases of human-to-human transmission of HPAI H5Nx have been documented to date, gain-of-function studies have shown that only a small number of mutations in the HA gene are required to render a reassortant H5Nx virus capable of droplet transmission in a ferret model (6, 7); notably, HA sequences isolated from recent H5 outbreaks have similar amino acid substitutions (8). Additionally, the potential for reassortment of genomic segments between avian and human influenza viruses can generate marked changes in the antigenicity of influenza viruses and presents a persistent risk for the emergence of novel pandemic viruses (9–11).

The influenza HA glycoprotein is synthesized as a single polypeptide chain but is proteolytically processed by host furin-like proteases into an HA1 “head” that mediates receptor binding and an HA2 stem which accommodates the viral fusion machinery. Humoral responses elicited after influenza infection or vaccination are often directed toward the variable HA head and are preferentially elicited relative to monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) recognizing the conserved HA stem domain (12); these head-directed antibodies often neutralize by blocking viral attachment, and correlate with protection (4). The preferential targeting of highly variable HA epitopes is referred to as antibody immunodominance and has been reproducibly observed after infection or vaccination in mice (13) and in humans (12, 14, 15); this observation extends even to lampreys, which have a non-immunoglobulin-based humoral immune system and diverged from mammals 550 million years ago (16). Naive B cell receptor (BCR) properties (e.g., affinity, precursor frequency) influence the outcome of a humoral response and immunodominance hierarchy. Recent adoptive transfer models using knock-in mice expressing BCRs of interest show that the competitive success of a naive B cell is dependent on precursor frequencies and affinity for antigen, whereby epitopes targeted by both higher affinity and frequency precursors had a selective advantage (17–20).

Traditional approaches for studying antigen-specific naive B cells include bioinformatic mining of available BCR datasets and inference of likely germline precursors by “germline-reverting” isolated mature BCR sequences; this is often limited by the availability of heavy and light chain paired sequence data and unreliable complementarity-determining region 3 (CDR3) loop approximation, respectively. Previously, we overcame these limitations by characterizing human naive B cells specific for the SARS-CoV-2 receptor binding domain (RBD) directly from the peripheral blood of seronegative donors to understand their relative abundance, intrinsic affinity, potential for activation and putative maturation pathways (21).

Here, we adapted this ex vivo approach to characterize the pre-pandemic H5 HA-specific naive B repertoire to compare the frequency, affinity, and neutralization potency between strain-specific B cells, and those naïve B cells that cross-react with an H1N1 that has been circulating in the human population. We found that H5-directed naïve B cells targeting the HA head domain are at an elevated frequency relative to cross-reactive H5/H1 B cells. By epitope mapping and structural analysis, we showed that naive antibodies engage H5 HA at key vulnerable sites previously defined by human antibodies elicited by natural infection and vaccination. Profiling human B cell specificities that recognize a pre-pandemic influenza(s) may inform our understanding of how precursor frequencies influence antibody immunodominance to HA, and potential de novo responses to zoonotic infection.

## RESULTS

### Analysis of HA-specific naive and memory B cells

Intrinsic patterns of immunodominance may be influenced by the frequency of naive precursors against a particular epitope on a complex antigen. Therefore, we sought to determine whether the naive repertoire is enriched for B cell clones specific for the globular H5 HA head relative to those targeting the conserved stem domain (Fig. 1A). We used a panel of recombinant HA probes and a flow cytometry gating strategy to differentiate between these specificities among human B cell samples (Fig. 1B and fig. S1D). We expressed HAs from a prototypical HPAI H5N1 strain, A/Vietnam/1203/2004 (VN04) as full-length soluble ectodomain (FLsE) and “head only” HA constructs. The FLsE HA from a contemporary human H1N1 strain, A/Michigan/45/2015 (MI15) was used in parallel to identify non-head, H1/H5 cross-reactive B cells (H1/H5). These HAs share ~53% and ~95% amino acid identity in the head and stem regions, respectively; H1 and H5 dual probe reactivity was previously performed to identify broadly neutralizing antibodies (bnAbs) targeting a conserved stem epitope (17, 22, 23).

Using these probes, we isolated naive (CD19+/IgD+/IgG−/CD27−) H5 HA head and H1/H5 cross-reactive B cells from the peripheral blood of 6 healthy human donors (HDs) in 2022. While there was low H5 head IgG serum titres across donors, given the low prevalence of H5Nx in the human population it is unlikely this was due to an H5Nx infection, but rather potential cross-reactive serum antibodies elicited by an H1N1 exposure (fig. S1A, B). Indeed, sera from selected human donors had no appreciable hemagglutination inhibition (HAI) activity against authentic H5N1 virus (fig. S1C). We defined H5 HA head-specific B cells that bound H5 FLsE, H5 head, but not to H1 FLsE (Fig. 1B, C and fig. S2). Conversely, we defined H1/H5 cross-reactivity as B cells that bound H5 and H1 FLsE probes, but not to H5 head (Fig. 1B, C). All 7 donors had detectable populations of head- and H1/H5-reactive naive B cells and the mean frequency was ~2.3-fold higher for head- (1:61,900) relative to H1/H5-reactive naive B cells (1:144,300) (Fig. 1B, G). Among H5 FLsE-reactive, naive cells, the median frequency of head-reactive clones was similarly elevated relative to H1/H5 clones at ~11.5% and ~5.6%, respectively (Fig. 1D).

For each donor, we also interrogated head and H1/H5 reactivity for class-switched immunoglobulin B cells (swIg; CD19+/IgM−/IgD−) using the same gating scheme described above (Fig. 1C and fig. S2). We detected an ~11-fold lower median frequency of H5 head reactive swIg B cells (0.0015%) relative to H1/H5 cells (0.017%), suggesting unlikely prior exposure to H5Nx and a pre-existing memory B cell population recognizing the stem region, which is conserved between H1 and H5 HAs (Fig. 1E). Indeed, primary exposure to a highly divergent strain such as H5N1 or the 2009 pandemic H1N1 strain showed recall of memory B cells toward conserved epitopes (22, 24–27). Upon re-exposure to the same strain (i.e., seasonal vaccination), the response, however, reverts to strain-specific head epitopes deriving from naive B cells (22, 25, 28).

To further characterize the H5-specific naive precursors, we obtained 88 paired heavy and light chain sequences from 4 of the 7 donors; these included 53 head-specific and 35 H1/H5 cross-reactive clones (Fig. 1F). All isolated clones were unique and derived from diverse heavy and light chains gene suggesting that a polyclonal pool of antibody precursors may be elicited upon antigen exposure. We found that 1) the IGHV3-21/IGKV4-1 gene pairing was observed in all four donors, representing ~25% of the sequenced H5 head-specific clones; 2) the heavy and light chain CDR3 lengths were normally distributed (34, 35) with no observed differences between HA specificities (fig. S3A); and 3) the majority of obtained sequences were fully germline confirming the sorted naive phenotype (fig. S3B).

Notably absent, however, from the cross-reactive H1/H5 naive sequences were the IGHV genes commonly associated with mAbs targeting the conserved HA stem epitope (e.g., IGHV1-69) (29). Thus, to compare the genetic diversity between H1/H5 naive and pre-existing H5-specific memory B cells, we single-cell sorted and sequenced H5-specifc naive and swIg B cells from two additional donors (fig. S4A, B). Cross-reactive H1/H5 naive BCRs had diverse IGHV genes with only 1 out of 16 sequences (~6%) using a canonical stem germline, IGHV1-18 (fig. S4C). Conversely, IGHV1-69 dominated the H1/H5 swIg B cell repertoire (~60%), consistent with previous reports of genetically restricted H1/H5 cross-reactivity (30, 31) (fig. S4D). Additionally, the stem mAb-associated gene, IGHV1-18, represented ~9% of the swIg cross-reactive repertoire (fig. S4D). As expected, swIg H1/H5 BCRs had increased heavy chain mutations relative to the naive BCRs; clonally related BCRs were also identified (fig. S4E). The lack of H1/H5 BCRs with canonical stem mAb IGHV isolated from the naive compartment may be due to low affinity to the HA probes used here (32); higher avidity probes may be required to isolate potential naive precursors (17) or affinity maturation may be necessary to acquire H5 HA binding breadth (29, 32).

### Naive antibodies engage broad H5 HAs

From the 53 head-specific and 35 H1/H5 cross-reactive paired sequences, we chose a representative 18 and 8 clones, respectively, across four donors for further characterization; these were downselected to maximize sequence diversity and length in the CDRs, particularly focusing on CDR H3, as well as heavy and light gene usage diversity; moreover, we selected antibodies from both the head-specific and cross-reactive populations to assess potential differences between epitope(s) (table S1).We first confirmed reactivity of the recombinantly produced mAbs in ELISA to the probes used for initial isolation: H5 VN04 head and FLsE as well as H1 MI15 FLsE; we used head-specific 5J8 and 13D4, as well as stem-directed MEDI8852, as control mAbs. (Fig. 2A). Next, we assessed breadth of the naïve mAbs across HPAI H5Nx clades. These viruses have a high degree of genetic diversity within the H5 HA gene due to long-term endemicity in avian hosts, as well as antibody-mediated selection contributing to its evolution (10, 33). H5Nx include clades and subclades, which are defined by the average percentage pairwise HA nucleotide when divergence exceed ~1.5% from a known clade (fig. S5A, B) (34). Thus, we recombinantly expressed representative H5 HAs from these diverse clades (fig. S5B) (35), including A/Astrakhan/3212/2020 and A/Colorado/18/2022 (clade 2.3.4..4b), which are closely related to currently circulating HPAI H5Nx strains (36, 37). We subsequently tested whether the naive mAbs isolated with H5 VN04 probes (clade 1) could recognize HAs from these diverse viruses (Fig. 2B). We found that ~95% of the mAbs with detectable H5 VN04 affinity also recognized the closely related A/Indonesia/5/2005 H5 HA (IN05; clade 2.1.3.2; ~96.6% amino acid identity) with decreasing cross-reactivity to HAs diverging from H5 VN04 (Fig. 2B). A subset (~25%) of the naive mAbs bound to HAs across all tested clades including head and H1/H5 cross-reactive clones, suggesting that a population of naive mAbs bound conserved HA epitopes (Fig. 2B). Despite high sequence homology in the stem region across tested H5 HAs, reactivity was limited for many of the cross-reactive H1/H5 naive clones suggesting potential sensitivity to non-head H5 HA amino acid differences.

Lastly, we assessed the polyreactivity of the isolated naive mAbs using classical self-antigens including dsDNA, cardolipin, and human insulin; polyreactivity was defined if an mAb reacted with two or more polyreactive antigens. We found that 6 of 15 H5 head-specific and 3 of 8 cross-reactive H1/H5 mAbs showed polyreactive binding (Fig. 2C). Such potential polyreactivity may also contribute to activation and selection of B cells upon antigenic exposure, in addition to precursor frequency and affinity.

### Naive antibodies engage vulnerable sites on the H5 HA head domain

To map the epitopes recognized by select naive neutralizing mAbs we first performed a competitive binding experiment by ELISA (38, 39). Naive mAbs were tested for competition against protective, neutralizing mAbs previously isolated from humans who recovered from HPAI H5N1 infection, 65C6 and 100F4 (40), and from mice immunized with HPAI H5N1, 13D4 and H5M9 (41, 42). Structural analysis of these antibody epitopes defined the four major vulnerable sites (VSs) on the H5 HA head (40) (Fig. 3A); stem-directed mAb, MEDI8852, was included in the competition assay as a negative control (43). The isolated naive mAbs competed with mAbs specific for VS2, VS3, and VS4 (Fig. 3B). Specifically, HD16_D07 competed with the vestigial esterase-specific antibody 100F4 (VS3), HD16_D04 competed with both 100F4 and H5M9, recognizing the upper and lower regions on the vestigial esterase domains (VS3 and VS4), and HD15_F06 competed with the receptor binding site (RBS)-specific antibody 13D4 (VS2). Minimal competition was detected against the lateral patch antibody, 65C6 (VS1), for these three naive mAbs. To more finely characterize the H5 HA antigenic sites recognized we performed epitope mapping studies using a mutagenized H5 HA head library displayed on the surface of yeast (44). In initial selection rounds we enriched for mutants that had a loss of binding phenotype (Fig. 3C, fig. S6). In the final round, clones were then positively selected for binding using defined, non-competitive and conformation-specific mAbs to ensure that enriched mutation(s) did not affect HA conformation (Fig. 3C). After sequencing single clones, isolated mutants were then displayed on the yeast-cell surface and assayed for binding to all three epitope-mapped naive mAbs (Fig. 3C). Naive mAb binding to mutant HAs was also compared to wild-type HA head binding to determine sensitivity to isolated variants, and subsequently mapped onto the H5 VN04 structure (Fig. 3D–F).

Mutations that abrogated binding of HD15_1F06 mAb mapped to positions in the RBS and corresponded to the VS2 region (Fig. 3A, C, D, E). VS2 has high sequence variability across H5 clades, including positions 155, 159, and 193, which may explain its limited breadth (Fig. 2B); notably, the latter position along with 226 affects human and avian receptor specificity (45). In H5Nx strains, Q226L is associated with enhanced binding to the receptor used by human-type HAs, α2,6-linked sialic acid (5, 46, 47). Loss of HD15_F06 binding to this variant suggests that this naive mAb may have a limited capacity to bind H5Nx viruses that acquire specificity for human receptor affinity.

For HD16_D07, variants were enriched around position 79, a conserved VS3 residue (Fig. 3A, C, and E). This upper vestigial esterase domain epitope partially overlaps with that of HD16_D04, where the latter variants (e.g., at position 267) reduce HD16_D07 binding as well. Mutations enriched throughout the vestigial esterase domain affected HD16_D04 binding, and map to both the VS3 and VS4 sites consistent with the competition ELISA (Fig. 4A, C, and F). While HD16_D04 does not directly compete with the RBS-directed 13D4 mAb in ELISA, it is sensitive to RBS mutations (e.g., residues 131, 155, and 193) in our yeast display platform. These naive mAbs targeting HA VSs isolated here may represent potential precursors for H5Nx neutralizing antibodies and appear to be similar to antibody responses observed after H5N1 natural infection (40) and vaccination (48).

### Structural characterization of a naive antibody in complex with H5 HA

To validate epitope mapping experiments and understand how a naive, neutralizing mAb binds to H5 HA, we determined the structure of HD16_D04 in complex with H5 VN04 FLsE by cryo-electron microscopy (cryoEM) (fig. S7, table S2). The structure determined at 3.1Å nominal resolution showed three Fabs per HA trimer and defined the epitope that overlaps with the vestigial esterase domain, with contact residues spanning both HA1 and HA2 (Fig. 4A). The interaction between HD16_D04 and HA is through both heavy and light chain contacts including significant contributions from germline encoded CDR1 and CDR2 (Fig. 4B). Key germline-encoded binding interactions with conserved HA residues include hydrogen-bonding contacts between Y31 (LCDR1) and the backbone carboxyl of P50 (HA), and between Y59 (HCDR2) and N276 (HA) (Fig. 4B, C). The cryoEM structure confirms that HD16_D04 binds an epitope positioned below but overlapping with previously defined vulnerable sites (VS3 and VS4), with contact residues shared between the protective mAbs H5M9 (42) and 100F4 (40), isolated from H5N1 immunized mice and a convalescent human donor, respectively (fig. S8). HD16_D04 epitope on VN04 HA includes residues that are broadly conserved across historical and contemporary H5 HA strains, likely contributing to its broad binding capacity (Fig. 2B).

### Naive antibodies recognizing the H5 HA head domain are neutralizing

We assessed the neutralization potency of select mAbs using an influenza reporter virus-based assay (49) (Fig. 5). Of the 26 germline mAbs, 9 (~35%) had detectable neutralization at 100 μg/ml when normalized to the virus-only control (Fig. 5A). These mAbs are predominantly H5 head-specific clones from diverse gene pairings and correlate between ELISA binding affinity and percent neutralization, with an EC50 range from ~0.10 -34.5 μg/ml (Fig. 5A–C). Three of the highest affinity head binding mAbs had IC50 values ranging from ~0.34 to 35.3 μg/ml (Fig. 5C). Notably, mAbs isolated after human infection or vaccination recognizing HA head epitopes tend to be more potently neutralizing than those recognizing the stem region (26, 49). Despite reduced potency relative to memory B-cell mAb controls (Fig. 5C), we identify naïve antibodies, within the human naive repertoire that can, at germline, neutralize a HPAI H5N1 virus; and represent a potential “first line” defense against a pre-pandemic virus.

## DISCUSSION

The naive B cell repertoire is the substrate for initial pathogen recognition. The composition and specificity of this diverse repertoire for a viral antigen are among the factors that influence outcome of a subsequent immune response. Here, we directly probed the specificity of the naive human B cell repertoire to understand how the immune system may respond upon primary exposure to a novel viral antigen, such as HPAI H5 HA. We identified genetically diverse naive BCRs that recognize both HA head and non-head epitopes; the former were observed with a consistently elevated frequency. Despite high genetic variability of H5 HAs, isolated naive mAbs bound diverse H5 clades including VSs epitopes defined by vaccine and infection-elicited mAbs.

Immunogenicity for a particular epitope may be influenced, in part, by the relative frequency of the corresponding BCR (18–20) resulting in dominant and subdominant humoral responses. To interrogate the potential preferential recognition and frequency of responses to the HA head relative to the stem domain, we designed a flow cytometry strategy to distinguish these specificities. We observed a greater frequency of germline BCRs specific for head relative to cross-reactive H1/H5 epitopes (>2-fold increase), which may contribute to preferential head-specific antibody responses. We can also approximate the mean frequency of H5 head- to H5 non-head specific naïve B cells (the latter encompassing the stem epitope), to 1 in ~61,900 and ~144,300, respectively; these were calculated based on total naïve B cells of 3-5 million per donor. Consistent with these approximations, a recent study showed that antibody titers for a subdominant stem epitope could be reproducibly amplified with a stem-only immunogen when the precursor frequency ratio between stem-specific and non-stem-epitopes was >1 (17, 20).

These precursor frequencies can vary based on epitope accessibility, valency, affinity, and avidity. Regarding epitope accessibility, we can approximate the solvent-accessible surface area (SASA) between the head and stem epitopes and in doing so there is only ~1.3 greater SASA from the head (~34,000Å2) relative to the stem relative to the stem (~25,420 Å2); this therefore does not appear to entirely account for our observation of ~2.3 fold greater frequency of head versus stem reactivity. There are also repertoire differences between individuals of different ages (50), ethnicities, and between host organisms (e.g., human, murine) (51, 52). For example, the results obtained here contrast a precursor frequency analysis performed in C57BL/6 mice (53) which showed that HA and stem precursor frequencies were highly similar (~1 in 4,000 naive B cells). However, there are several key differences: 1) a different set of flow-cytometry probes (H1 and H5 HA FLsE only) were used; 2) and at a lower HA concentration (8nM versus 25nM); and 3) a protein kinase inhibitor was used to reduce BCR internalization. Additionally, it is worth noting that the naive repertoires of C57BL/6 mice have on average, a shorter CDR3 length and a lower overall diversity (51, 52).

HA head-specific mAbs, particularly those that engage the RBS, can neutralize even with low binding affinity to the target antigen (54). Furthermore, the neutralizing humoral response to infection or vaccination is mediated primarily by HA head-specific mAbs (40). Consistent with these observations, we detected H5N1 neutralization for a subset of the isolated, head-specific naive mAbs, but not for the cross-reactive H1/H5 mAbs; such germline responses within the human repertoire is proposed to serve as an “innate-like” response to rapidly respond to pathogens (55).

While we identified naïve antibodies from immune repertoires that were specific to influenza HA, our study was limited in the number of human donors analyzed; increasing the number would improve the robustness and the power analyses regarding the frequency of gene usage. Furthermore, the immune status of these donors is unknown: because we do not have their genetic information, we cannot exclude that any of the donors was affected by a primary immunodeficiency, which would have, consequently, influenced their naïve B cell repertoire composition and/or frequencies. Additionally, we do not know if or how a donor’s immune exposure history to influenza could affect their naïve B cell repertoire and thus, a longitudinal sampling of individuals beginning with their first vaccination or infection may describe naïve repertoire dynamics in response to a viral antigen. Lastly, additional structural characterization of the isolated antibodies to more finely map the epitope(s) targeted will advance our understanding of the specificity of the naïve repertoire.

Collectively, these data highlight that humoral responses within the naïve repertoire that require no, or minimal somatic hypermutation, can both bind and neutralize pre-pandemic HPAI H5Nx viruses (56, 57); potentially offering protection. Understanding how the human naive repertoire could recognize potential zoonotic threats, may identify precursors for vaccine- or infection-specific naive B cells. Furthermore, these data advance our understanding of basic B cell biology and antibody immunodominance of the naïve repertoire.

## MATERIALS AND METHODS

### Study Design

The aim of this study was to analyze the human naive B cell repertoire specific for influenza hemagglutinin, the major target of neutralizing antibodies. We isolated naive B cells from the peripheral blood of 7 human donors, sequenced the BCRs, and recombinantly expressed a diverse panel of IgGs from 4 of these donors for subsequent biochemical characterization. Sample sizes for each experiment are indicated in the figure legends.

### Donor Samples

PBMCs for single cell sorting were isolated from 7 blood donors from the MGH blood donor center. Prior to donation, subjects signed a donor consent statement, stating ‘‘I give permission for my blood to be used for transfusion to patients or for research’’. The gender as well as the age/developmental stage of the patients is not recorded by the MGH blood donor center, however eligible donors must be a minimum of 16 years of age and weigh a minimum of 110lbs. All experiments were conducted with MGH Institutional Biosafety Committee approval (MGH protocol 2014B000035). B cell isolation was performed on donor samples in April and May of 2022.

### Expression and purification of recombinant HA antigens

Plasmids encoding the full-length soluble ectodomain (FLsE) of influenza HA (residues 15-522; H5 numbering) and head only constructs (residues 39-330; H5 numbering) were designed for H1 A/Michigan/45/2015, H5 A/Vietnam/1203/2004, H5 A/Indonesia/5/2005, H5 A/Egypt/N03072/2010, H5 A/Hubei/1/2010, H5 A/Anhui/1/2005, H5 A/Guizhou/1/2013, H5 A/Astrakhan/3212/2020, H5 A/gyrfalcon/Washington/41088-6/2014, H5 A/Guangdong/18SF020/2018, H5 A/Colorado/18/2022. Constructs were codon optimized and synthesized by IDT. FLsE and head only HA and constructs were cloned into pVRC8400 protein expression vectors with a C-terminal foldon or GCN4 trimerization tag, a HRV 3C-cleavable 8xHis tag, and AviTag. Monomeric HA head constructs were also cloned into pVRC vectors without a trimerization tag. Proteins were transiently expressed in Expi293F cells (ThermoFisher). 5 to 7 days post-transfection, supernatants were harvested by centrifugation and purified using cobalt-TALON resin (Takara) followed by size exclusion chromatography on a Superdex 200 Increase 10/300 GL column (GE Healthcare).

### Expression and purification IgGs and Fabs

IgG and Fab genes for the heavy- and light-chain variable domains were synthesized, and codon optimized by IDT and subcloned into pVRC8400 protein expression vectors and sequence confirmed (Genewiz). Fabs and IgGs were similarly expressed and purified as described above for HAAs. IgGs were buffer exchanged into PBS while Fabs were further purified by size exclusion chromatography (58). Amino acid sequences of the recombinantly expressed mAbs are provided in supplementary data file S1.

### ELISA

Sera and monoclonal antibody reactivity to HA antigens were assayed by ELISA. Briefly, 96-well high binding (Corning) were coated with 5 μg/ml of HAs in PBS at 100μl/well and incubated overnight at 4°C. Plates were blocked with 1% BSA in PBS containing 1% Tween-20 (PBS-T) for 1hr at room temperature (RT). Blocking solution was discarded and 4-fold serial dilutions of human plasma (1:20 starting dilution) or isolated monoclonal antibodies (150 μg/ml starting concentration) in PBS were added to wells and incubated for 1hr at RT. Plates were washed three times with PBS-T. Secondary, anti-human IgG-HRP (Abcam), was added at 1:20,000 dilution in PBS-T for 1hr at RT. Plates were washed three times with PBS-T and developed with 1-Step Slow TMB-ELISA (ThermoFisher). Absorbance was measured using a plate reader at 450nm. EC50 values were determined by non-linear regression (sigmoidal) using GraphPad Prism 8.4.3 software. ELISAs to establish H5 HA binding breadth were done at a single IgG concentration (100 μg/ml) in replicate. Positive binding was defined by an OD450 ≥ 0.50.

Polyreactivity ELISA plates against human insulin (MilliporeSigma) and dsDNA (Calf Thymus DNA; Invitrogen) were coated with 2 and 50 μg/ml, respectively, in PBS and incubated overnight at 4°C. Plates were blocked and incubated with IgGs as described above. Cardiolipin ELISAs were measured as previously described (59). Briefly, plates were coated with 5μg per well of cardiolipin (from bovine heart; MilliporeSigma; C1649) in 30μl ethanol uncovered overnight 4°C. Plates were washed twice with 100μl per well of 1x PBS and blocked with 100μl PBS + 10% FBS for 1 hour at room temperature (covered). Blocked plates were washed three times with 1x PBS and incubated with IgGs diluted in 1x PBS + 1% FBS for 1 hours at room temperature. After washing with 1x PBS, cardiolipin ELISAs were developed as described above. Polyreactive ELISAs were performed at a single IgG concentration (50 μg/ml) in duplicate and polyreactivity was defined by an OD450 ≥ 0.40 for two or more polyreactive antigens.

### Competition ELISAs

Competition ELISAs were performed as previously described (39). Briefly, detection antibodies (naive and published IgGs with known structures) were biotinylated with EZ-Link Sulfo-NHS-LC-Biotin (ThermoFisher) according to manufacturer’s protocol. 96-well high binding microplates (Corning) were coated with H5 FLsE at 5 μg/mL (in PBS) overnight at 4°C. Plates were blocked with 4% BSA in PBS containing 1% Tween-20 (PBS-T) for 120 min at room temperature (RT). Blocking solution was discarded and 25 μL of competing IgGs were added onto the plate at 200μg/mL. An equivalent volume of biotinylated IgG was then added at 5μg/mL and incubated for 90 min at RT. Plates were washed three times with PBS-T. Secondary, HRP-conjugated streptavidin (ThermoFisher), was added at 1:5,000 dilution in PBS (150uL/well) for 1hr at RT. After this point, the protocol was identical to the standard ELISA method. A no-competition control was used for comparison to assess binding loss from competition, and percent loss was computed relative to this control. Negative values were treated as 0% competition.

### Probe generation

Avi-tagged FLsE and trimeric head constructs were biotinylated using a BirA biotin-protein ligase kit (Avidity) according to manufacturer’s protocol and subsequently repurified by size exclusion chromatography on a Superdex 200 Increase 10/300 GL column (GE Healthcare) in PBS. All HA constructs for sorting contained a Y98F mutation to prevent non-specific binding to sialic acid (23). Biotinylated HAs were individually premixed with fluorescently labeled streptavidin (SA) at a 4:1 molar ratio to for 30 min at 4 °C prior to sorting to form fluorescent antigen tetramers (60). H5 FLsE-Fd was mixed SA-APC, H5 FLsE-GCN4 or SA-APC, H5 Head-Fd was mixed with SA-BV421, and H1 FLsE-Fd was mixed with SA-BV650. Two different trimerization tags were used for H5 FLsE probes to avoid tag-specific, off-target B cell binding.

Naive B cells were purified from PBMCs using the MACS Human B Cell isolation kit (Miltenyi Biotec) and incubated with 25nM of each HA probe (H5-FLsE-Fd-APC, H5-FLsE-GCN4-PE, H5-Head-Fd-BV421, and H1-FLsE-BV650) for 30 min at 4°C in PBS + 5μM biotin to quench free biotin binding sites and avoid streptavidin cross probe binding. Cells were stained with anti-human CD19 (Alexa-700; BioLegend, cat. no 302226), CD3 (APC/Cy7; BioLegend, cat no. 300426), IgD (PerCP-Cy5.5; BD Biosciences, cat no. 561315), IgG (BV711; BD Biosciences, cat no. 740796), IgM (BV605; BioLegend, cat no. 314523), CD27 (BV510; BD Biosciences, cat no. 750167), CD45RB (FITC; BioLegend, cat no. 310206), and LiveDead NearIR (Invitrogen), for an additional 30 min at 4°C. Plates were stored at −80 °C for subsequent analysis. 3-6 million events were recorded for each sample for antigen-specific frequency determination and the remainder of the sample was single cell sorted. Flow cytometry data was analyzed using FlowJo software version 10.7.1.

### B cell receptor sequencing

BCR Sequencing was carried out as described previously (61). Briefly, thawed B cell lysates are reverse transcribed with SuperScript IV (ThermoFisher) and random hexamer primers. Heavy and light chain sequences are amplified with Platinum Taq DNA polymerase (ThermoFisher) utilizing openPrimeR optimized primer sets for the amplification of all human IGH, IGK, and IGL immunoglobulin V gene segments optimized (62). In a single first-round multiplex PCR, heavy and light-chain sequences are amplified simultaneously. In a second, semi-nested PCR reaction, heavy and light chains variable regions are amplified separately, analyzed by agarose gel electrophoresis, and submitted for Sanger sequencing (Azenta). Sequences were analyzed using IMGT High V-Quest.

### Generation of H5N1 reporter virus

A reporter virus encoding the fluorescent protein tdKatushka2 in place of the PB1 segment was generated as previously described (49). HEK293T cells were seeded at 6 x 105 cells per well. The next day (~18 hours), the HEK293T cells were transfected using TransIT-LT1 (Mirus bio) complexed with 0.5 μg of each of the following plasmids containing the six internal segments from A/WSN/1933 in the pHW2000 backbone, an N1 A/Vietnam/1203/2004 in the pHW2000 backbone, tdKatushka2 flanked with PB1 packing sequences in the pHW2000 backbone, an H5 A/Vietnam/1203/2004 expression plasmid, and a plasmid to express TMPRSS2 to activate HA. The H5 HA expression plasmid does not generate viral RNA, allowing the reporter virus to be handled safely at BSL2, but requiring passaging in a cell line expressing the HA (MDCK-SIAT1-H5). Three days after transfection, the supernatant was spun at 800 x g for 5 minutes to remove dead cells and cell debris. The supernatant was then used to infect a confluent monolayer of MDCK-SIAT1-H5 cells (plated the day before at 6 x 105 cells per well). Three days after infection, the supernatant was recovered as before and further passaged on MDCK-SIAT1-H5 cells in T75 flasks. Three days after this infection, the virus was frozen in 0.5 ml aliquots at −70C.

### Titering and neutralization of H5N1 reporter virus

The H5N1 viral stocks were titered on Madin-Darby canine kidney (MDCK)-SIAT1-H5 cells. The day before infection, 20,000-30,000 MDCK-SIAT1-H5 cells were seeded in 96-well plates (CellVis) in flu media (OptiMEM supplemented with 0.3% BSA, calcium chloride, magnesium chloride, and penicillin/streptomycin). Prior to infection, the virus was diluted in flu media additionally supplemented with 2 μg/ml TPCK-trypsin (Sigma) in a 2-fold dilution series across a U-bottom 96-well plate (Corning) and then mixed with an equal volume of flu media for titeringor containing a 2X concentration of antibody for neutralization. After 1h incubation at 37C/5% CO2, the media was removed from the MDCK-SIAT1-H5 cells and replaced with 100 μL of the virus or virus/antibody mixture. Approximately 18-20 hours after infection, the plates were analyzed on a CellDiscoverer7 (Zeiss) by detecting infected cells determined by the fluorescence of tdKatushka2. The resulting images were analyzed by the Zeiss Zen Blue software by counting the number of infected cells. For titering, cell counts were plotted and analyzed in GraphPad Prism by fitting a sigmoidal curve. The dilution corresponding to the inflection point was used for neutralization assays. For neutralization assays, a virus only control (0% neutralization) and a cell only control (100% neutralization) were performed in at least quadruplicate. Neutralization was calculated by subtracting the background (cell control) from the cell count and dividing by the virus control with the background subtracted: 100 x [1-(cell count of well – cell count of cell only control)/(cell count of virus control – cell count of cell only control)]. Assay was performed in duplicates (for 100μg single-hit) or quadruplicates (for IgG titrations; 150μg/ml starting concentration with 4-fold dilutions in flu media). Data were analyzed using Graphpad Prism.

### Hemagglutination Inhibition Assay

Hemagglutination inhibition (HAI) was performed as described previously (31, 63). Briefly, sera were treated overnight with receptor destroying enzyme (RDE) (0.1mg/ml) at 37°C, according to the manufacturer’s specifications (RDE; Denka-Seiken). The mixtures were then incubated at 56°C to inactivate the RDE (3 hours). For HAI, the samples were serially diluted twofold through 1:256 in v-bottom 96 well plates. Low pathogenicity H5N1 virus (A/Vietnam/2008) (17, 64) was diluted to 8 HAU/ 50μl and then added to the diluted serum (1:1). The serum-virus mixture was incubated at room temperature for 45 minutes while shaking. Chicken red blood cells (RBCs) (Lampire Biological Laboratories) were diluted a concentration of 0.5% in PBS and added to the serum-virus mixture and incubated for 30 minutes at room temperature. Additional controls included: serial dilution of the H5N1 virus input solution without sera to reconfirm hemagglutination titer; incubation of H5N1 without serum; and incubation of 0.5% RBCs in PBS without virus.

### Epitope mapping by yeast display

Mutagenized yeast display libraries for the VN04 HA head were generated as described above, by error-prone PCR with an estimated library size at ~5 x 107 as determined by the number of colonies that grew on SDCAA plates. Displayed wild-type VN04 HA head was used as a control to draw the gates for the negative selection of mutant libraries. For the first two rounds, induced wild-type HA or mutant HA libraries were stained with an anti-H5 naive antibody at 100nM in PBSF and chicken anti-c-myc IgY (1:500). Following two washes in PBSF, wild-type HA or mutant HA libraries were stained with secondary antibodies: anti-chicken IgY AF488 (1:500) and anti-human IgG AF647 antibody (Jackson ImmunoResearch, Dilution: 1:300). After one wash with PBSF, clones displaying loss-binding mutants relative to wild-type HA were sorted and cultured for subsequent rounds of selection. In the third round, wild-type HA or mutant HA libraries were stained with ≥2 non-competitive IgGs (as established by competition ELISA) and mutant clones that stained at similar levels to wild-type HA were sorted (positive selection) and plated on SDCAA agar plates. Colonies were picked (24/library) for Sanger sequencing and HA mutations were mapped onto the H5 HA structure (PDB: 2FK0). Single clones from the final round of sorting were induced in deep 96-well plates and stained/detected as described above using 50nM IgG. Antibody binding was normalized to cmyc expression by gating in FlowJo, and loss of binding was determined by comparing IgG binding signal relative to wild-type HA for each antibody tested as a percentage: (normalized mutant AF647 MFI / normalized wild-type AF647 MFI) x 100%.

### CryoEM sample preparation and data collection

The rHA FLsE of H5/Vietnam/1204/2004 was incubated with the HD16-D04 Fab at a molar ratio 1:1.5 and a final protein concentration of 2.5mg/mL for 40 minutes on ice. Immediately before depositing the sample onto Au Flat GF-0.6/1.0-3Au 45nm-50 grids (Electron Microscopy Sciences), octy-beta-glucoside was added to the pre-formed complex at 0.083% (w/v) final concentration. Plasma cleaning of the grids was performed with a Solarus plasma cleaner machine (Gatan) for 7 seconds (O2/Ar). 3μL of the sample were applied on the gold face of the grids, blotted for 6 seconds on the same face of the grid, at 20° C and 100% humidity, then plunge-frozen in 100% liquid ethane using a LEICA EM GP2 plunge freezer. The grids were first screened on an Artica Talos microscope equipped with a Gatan K3 camera and operated at 200 kV. The highest quality grid was then imaged using a Titan Krios microscope operated at 300 kV and equipped with a Gatan K3 Summit direct electron detector. A total of 17,120 movies were collected in counting mode at 30 e-/px/s for a total dose of 58.49 e−/Å2/s. Images were collected at a magnification of 81000, corresponding to a calibrated pixel size of 0.846 Å/pixel. Defocus values ranged between −1 and −2.5 μm.

### CryoEM data processing

The data were processed using cryoSPARC v4.3.1 (65) (fig. S7, table S1). Briefly, the movies were aligned and corrected for both global and local motion using Patch Motion Correction within cryoSPARC. Then, contrast transfer function estimation was done using Patch CTF and particles were picked using blob picker. The picked particles were extracted with a box size 400 pixels and 4x binned for 2D classification. Two rounds of 2D classification were performed and 557,829 particles were selected for the generation of the initial model at 12 Å/pixel with 3 classes. Non-uniform refinement was performed in C1 symmetry for each individual class. The particles from the best class were re-extracted with a box size of 400 pixels and binned 2x and then subject to 3D classification into 5 classes with a target resolution of 4Å. The particles from the top 3 classes were combined and used for non-uniform refinement and local CTF refinement with the best volume obtained from the 3D classification. The particle stack from the local CTF refinement was then used for new round of non-uniform refinement, and then a new round of 3D classification was performed with 3 classes at a target resolution of 3Å. The 3 classes were subject to a new round of non-uniform refinement. The final class contained 77,276 particles. Local CTF refinement was then performed this particle stack and then subjected to a new round of non-uniform refinement with C3 symmetry imposed. A new round of local CTF refinement followed by non-uniform refinement in C3 symmetry was performed and then subject to global CTF refinement follow by new round of non-uniform refinement in C3 symmetry. The particles were re-extracted at full box size of 400 pixels without binning and a new round of non-uniform refinement and local CTF refinement was performed. This particle stack was used for a last non-uniform refinement with C3 symmetry and yielded a reconstruction at 3.1Å nominal resolution. The two half-maps were used for sharpening in DeepEMhancer (66). The reported resolution is based on the gold-standard Fourier shell correlation of 0.143 criterion. (See table S1)

### Model building and refinement

The DeepEMhancer sharpened map was used for model building. The HA trimer from PDB 7DEB and the variable region of the D04 Fab, predicted with SABPred (67), were manually docked into the map using UCSF ChimeraX (68) and then manually built using COOT (69). N-linked glycans were built manually in COOT using the glyco extension and their stereochemistry and fit to the map validated with Privateer (70). The model was then refined in Phenix (71) using real-space refinement and validated with MolProbity (72) (See table S1). The structural biology software was compiled and distributed by SBGrid (73).
